podcast.title: Tragic Death in Car Crash (February 6, 1960)
podcast.body: Jesse Belvin died instantly in a car crash on February 6, 1960, shortly after performing at a concert in Little Rock, Arkansas. His wife, Joanne, who he reportedly shielded from the worst of the impact, was seriously injured and succumbed to her injuries a few days later. The circumstances of their deaths are shrouded in rumor and lack of official investigation due to institutional racism at the time. "On February the 6th, 1960, there was a concert in Little Rock, Arkansas at the Robinson Auditorium."

podcast.title: Abandoning The Cliques' Success
podcast.body: After forming The Cliques with Eugene Church, their song "The Girl in My Dreams" reached number 45 on the Pop Chart, a clear commercial success. However, Belvin made the decision to abandon the group name and pursue a solo career rather than capitalize on or follow up on this minor hit. "And so of course, at this point, Belvin ditched the Cliques name, rather than follow up on the minor hit, and started making records as a solo artist instead."

podcast.title: Advice on Royalties
podcast.body: Jesse Belvin taught Richard Berry that musicians in the 1950s rarely received royalties from recording contracts, regardless of their terms, influencing Berry's strategy to prioritize session fees. "he'd learned from Jesse Bellvin that it didn't matter what the contract said, you were never going to get any royalties when you made records."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Cavalier Attitude Towards Songwriting Credit
podcast.body: Jesse Belvin frequently sold his songwriting rights for as little as $100, often resulting in him not receiving label credit for his compositions. This "cavalier attitude" is exemplified by the alleged sale of the bridge he wrote for "Good Night My Love" to John Mariscalco for $400, reflecting his focus on immediate cash over long-term royalties. "Most of the time, he would also be writing the songs, but he didn't get label credits on most of them, because he would just sell all his rights to the songs for $100."

podcast.title: Central Avenue Music Scene Involvement
podcast.body: Jesse Belvin was an active participant in the Central Avenue music scene in Los Angeles, where Sam Cooke also spent time before Keen Records was fully established. "Sam made himself firmly a part of the central avenue music scene, hanging around with Gaynell Hodge, Jesse Belvin, Dutti Williams, Guggi Renne, John Dolphin, and everyone else who was part of the LAR and B community."

podcast.title: Children Raised by Grandmother
podcast.body: Jesse and Joanne Belvin left behind two children under the age of five, who were subsequently raised by Jesse's mother. Their oldest son, Jesse Belvin Jr., later became a singer himself, performing his father's material and dedicating his life to uncovering the truth behind his parents' mysterious deaths, though he never found definitive answers. "When they died, they left behind two children under the age of five who were brought up by Jesse's mother."

podcast.title: Commercial Success at Specialty
podcast.body: Jesse Belvin was one of the Specialty Records acts who were experiencing considerable commercial success, with sales described as "hand-over-fist." "other specialty acts, like Lloyd Price, Jesse Belvin, and guitar slim, were all selling hand-over-fist."

podcast.title: Drafted into Armed Forces
podcast.body: Jesse Belvin's burgeoning career was set back when he was drafted into the Armed Forces shortly after the success of "Dream Girl" with Jesse and Marvin. While serving, a song he co-wrote, "Earth Angel," became a hit, though he initially received no credit for his contribution. "But shortly afterwards, Belvin was drafted."

podcast.title: Impact of Gaynell Hodge
podcast.body: Gaynell Hodge was an essential figure in the 1950s LA vocal group scene, and his fundamental contributions meant that without him, Jesse Belvin would not have existed. "without him there would been no platters, penguins, or Jesse Bellvin."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Influence and Esteem Among Peers
podcast.body: In the 1950s R&B scene, particularly on the West Coast, Jesse Belvin was considered an unparalleled figure among musicians, possessing immense potential to be a bigger star than anyone. Stevie Wonder cited him as his favorite singer, and Etta James vocally advocated for his inclusion in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, considering his exclusion a travesty. Sam Cooke explicitly modeled his career after Belvin's. "But in 1950s R&B among musicians, especially those on the West Coast, there was no bigger name than Jesse Belvin."

podcast.title: Joanne Belvin's Management and Songwriting
podcast.body: Jesse Belvin's wife, Joanne, became his manager and songwriting partner, taking firm control of his career in 1958. Her influence led to his signing with RCA and a strategic shift towards a smooth ballad singing style, aiming for mainstream stardom in the vein of Nat King Cole. She notably wrote the hit song "Guess Who" based on a love letter to him. "But his wife also became his songwriting partner and his manager, and in 1958 she seemed to finally take control of his career for him."

podcast.title: Mentor to The Flamingos
podcast.body: Jesse Belvin, who was a couple of years older than its members, served as a partigé to the group The Flamingos. "partigés of Jesse Belvin, who was a couple of years older than them."

podcast.title: Misinformation and Historical Obscurity
podcast.body: Jesse Belvin's career is plagued by inaccuracies and a general lack of information, often relegating him to a footnote in the biographies of other artists. For instance, the false claim that Barry White played piano on "Good Night My Love" persisted despite White being only eleven at the time of the song's release. "But that kind of misinformation is all over everything to do with Jesse Belvin."

podcast.title: Prolific Career and Aliases
podcast.body: Jesse Belvin was an exceptionally prolific songwriter, performer, and group leader who released an astonishing number of records under so many different names that it is challenging to ascertain the full extent of his career. Despite his widespread influence and immense potential for stardom, this complexity contributed to him being an often-overlooked figure in music history. "He put out a truly astonishing number of records as a songwriter, performer and group leader, under so many different names that it's impossible to figure out the true extent of his career."

podcast.title: Samuel Brown's Tutelage
podcast.body: Like many R&B and Jazz greats, Jesse Belvin attended Jefferson High School and studied music under Samuel Brown. Brown, a significant but often uncredited figure, also taught other notable musicians like Big Jay McNeely and is recognized as an "unsung hero of rock and roll music." "Belvin had attended Jefferson High School and studied music under the great teacher Samuel Brown, who is one of the great on-song heroes of rock and roll music."

podcast.title: Slow Dancing Favorite
podcast.body: Jesse Belvin was an artist whose music was particularly popular on early Jamaican sound systems for slow dancing occasions. "and for slow dancing the moon blows and Jesse Belvin."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Uninvestigated Death and Sabotage Rumors
podcast.body: Following the fatal car crash that killed Jesse and Joanne Belvin, no thorough investigation was conducted due to institutional racism prevalent in the Deep South at the time. Rumors quickly circulated, including newspaper reports of slashed tires on Belvin's car, unconfirmed death threats against Belvin, and car troubles experienced by Jackie Wilson and other musicians on the same night, leading to speculation of sabotage or racist murder. "So when Jesse and Joanne Belvin died, they could have been the victims of a racist murder, or they could just have been horribly unlucky."
